lesson_title: Fetch, Swap, Carry, Swap, Burn: The Journey of One Breath
hook_text: Breathing is not respiration. Your toes respire. Your brain respires. Your lungs never do.
clip_script: Three jobs, one confusing word. Fetching: that is breathing, the diaphragm and ribs pushing air in and out of your chest. Just moving air. Swapping: down in the alveoli, oxygen hops from the air into the blood and carbon dioxide hops out, by diffusion, from where there is more to where there is less. Nobody pushes. Burning: in the mitochondria of every single cell, glucose plus oxygen gives carbon dioxide plus water plus energy. That is respiration, and it happens in your toes, your brain, a leaf, a fish. Never in the lungs. The lungs only swap. Why are the alveoli so good at swapping? Three hundred million wet grapes, half a tennis court of surface, walls one cell thick, wrapped in a net of moving blood that keeps the difference big. Feature, then reason. Now sprint. Breathing jumps from 15 to 40, heart from 70 to 150, fetching and carrying more oxygen every minute. Not enough? Your muscles burn glucose without oxygen and leave lactic acid: that is the fire in your thighs. Fetch, swap, carry, swap, burn.
visual_style: Three verbs stamp across the screen; air flows into a chest, oxygen dots hop across a thin wall into a red stream, ride to a thigh and vanish into a glowing mitochondrion; a sprinter's legs glow red with lactic acid.
pacing: Three equal verb beats, a quick four-feature list, an accelerating sprint, a five-word finish.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and recite the nine stops from air to cell and back.
